verses.text: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the reports about Jesus
and said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him."
Now Herod had arrested John and bound him and put him in prison on account of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife,
because John had been telling him, "It is not lawful for you to have her."
Although Herod wanted to kill John, he was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet.
On Herod's birthday, however, the daughter of Herodias danced before them and pleased Herod
so much that he promised with an oath to give to her whatever she asked.
Prompted by her mother, she said, "Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist."
The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests, he ordered that her wish be granted
and sent to have John beheaded in the prison.
John's head was brought in on a platter and presented to the girl, who carried it to her mother.
Then John's disciples came and took his body and buried it. And they went and informed Jesus.
When Jesus heard about John, He withdrew by boat privately to a solitary place. But the crowds found out about it and followed Him on foot from the towns.
When He stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them and healed their sick.
When evening came, the disciples came to Him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the hour is already late. Dismiss the crowds so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food."
"They do not need to go away," Jesus replied. "You give them something to eat."
"We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish," they answered.
"Bring them here to Me," Jesus said.

And He directed the crowds to sit down on the grass. Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, He spoke a blessing. Then He broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people.
They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
About five thousand men were fed, besides women and children.
Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to the other side, while He dismissed the crowds.
After He had dismissed them, He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray. When evening came, He was there alone,
but the boat was already far from land, buffeted by the waves because the wind was against it.
During the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea.
When the disciples saw Him walking on the sea, they were terrified. "It's a ghost!" they said, and cried out in fear.
But Jesus spoke up at once: "Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid."
"Lord, if it is You," Peter replied, "command me to come to You on the water."
"Come," said Jesus. Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water, and came toward Jesus.
But when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, "Lord, save me!"
Immediately Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter. "You of little faith," He said, "why did you doubt?"
And when they had climbed back into the boat, the wind died down.
Then those who were in the boat worshiped Him, saying, "Truly You are the Son of God!"
When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret.
And when the men of that place recognized Jesus, they sent word to all the surrounding region. People brought all the sick to Him
and begged Him just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.

context.author: Matthew, writing to a Jewish audience
context.genre: Narrative — a flashback account of John's execution, followed by two of Jesus' best-known miracles.
context.audience: Jewish-Christian readers watching John's fate foreshadow Jesus' own coming suffering under a weak ruler swayed by political pressure.
context.mapLabel: GALILEE — A SOLITARY SHORE, THEN GENNESARET
context.setting: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea (4 BC-AD 39) from his capital Tiberias, on the Sea of Galilee. His marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife, broke Leviticus 18:16 — John's public rebuke of that marriage is what led to his imprisonment and death.
context.custom: Herod's oath, made rashly in front of dinner guests, obligated him by the social expectations of the time to honor it publicly even after regretting it — a dynamic Matthew highlights as a real constraint, not merely royal whim.
context.timelineImmediate: Opens with news of John's execution reaching Jesus, prompting Him to withdraw — but the crowds follow, leading directly into the feeding of the five thousand and the walking on water, two of the most well-attested miracles across all four Gospels.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' declaration "It is I" (v.27) is, in Greek, the same phrase (egō eimi) God uses to reveal His name in Exodus 3:14 — a subtle but direct echo tying this moment to God's self-revelation at the burning bush.

translation.meaning: A visceral, gut-level empathy — Jesus ministers to the crowd even while presumably still grieving John's death.

occurrences.note: Used only for Jesus Himself, or for a clear Christ-figure in three of His parables — the good Samaritan, the forgiving master, and the father of the prodigal son.

translation.meaning: The same self-identifying phrase God uses in Exodus 3:14 — likely more than a simple "it's me," carrying divine resonance.
A command to be bold or of good cheer — the same word Jesus uses elsewhere when reassuring the fearful.

occurrences.note: Always spoken as a command, never a description — five times by Jesus, once by the risen Lord to Paul, and once echoed back by a crowd.

translation.meaning: To waver or hesitate between two decisions — describes Peter's divided attention between Jesus and the wind, not outright disbelief.

occurrences.note: Used only twice in the whole New Testament, and both times in Matthew alone — here with Peter on the water, and again with the disciples on the mountain after the resurrection.

gospelParallels.note: Mark's fuller account of John's death, with more detail on Herod's inner conflict.
John's version of the feeding of the five thousand, leading into His "Bread of Life" discourse.
Mark's parallel account of walking on water, without the detail of Peter stepping out of the boat.

otBackground.note: The law against marrying a brother's wife, which John's rebuke of Herod was built on.
Elisha's smaller-scale bread multiplication miracle, a precedent for the feeding of the five thousand.
God described as treading on the sea and stilling storms — background for Jesus walking on water and calming the wind.

context.sparkNotes: Herod beheads John the Baptist, and Jesus withdraws — only to feed five thousand and walk on water that same night. "Doubt," used to describe Peter sinking on the water, appears only twice in the whole New Testament, both times in Matthew alone — and Jesus walking on the sea echoes Job 9:8's picture of God treading the waves.

commentary.note: Henry catches Herod's hollow, superstitious guilt precisely: "the devils believe and tremble, but they never believe and repent" — terror of conscience without any real change of heart. He also notes the timing isn't accidental: crowds pressed harder toward Jesus after John's martyrdom than before, since "the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church."

JFB catches a precise nuance in Peter's Greek that's easy to miss in translation — he doesn't ask Jesus to "let" him come, but to "command" him, using the language of an order rather than a permission. Read that way, his request looks less like impulsive boldness and more like a deliberate act of submission to whatever Jesus would say.

Clarke argues that when Jesus "blessed" the loaves, the object of that blessing was God Himself, not the bread — following standard Jewish custom of blessing the Giver rather than the gift. He also stresses the scale of the miracle plainly: five loaves fed five thousand men (plus women and children), with twelve baskets of fragments left over — more surplus than the entire original supply.
